analysis.one_liner: Phases out Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's mortgage guarantees, sells their assets to private firms, and rewrites mortgage rules.
analysis.headline: The bill got a single Senate Banking Committee hearing in November 2011 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would start shrinking the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guarantee by at least 10% a year and direct the government to sell the two companies' databases, price indices, and securitization technology to private firms. It would require every regulated mortgage lender to publish detailed loan-level performance data publicly, set a nationwide minimum 5% down payment with verified income, and standardize how loans are serviced and how foreclosures are handled. It would also repeal the Dodd-Frank rule requiring lenders who bundle loans into securities to keep a share of the risk, and exempt some private mortgage-backed securities from securities registration rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Private lenders, securitizers, and mortgage investors gain the most: they get free access to loan-level data across the market, a repeal of the rule making them keep 5% of the credit risk on loans they package and sell, an exemption from securities registration for 'deliverable residential mortgage' securities, and the chance to buy Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's proprietary data and technology. Struggling borrowers also get real protections: a single point of contact, uniform standards pushing loan modification over foreclosure, and national foreclosure rules. Homebuyers with strong finances get clearer underwriting rules, but buyers who need a low down payment lose access.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private lenders, investors, and mortgage securitizers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every regulated mortgage lender to publish detailed, continuously updated loan-level data — origination terms, payments, delinquencies, fees — into the public domain, which gives investors and analysts the information to price mortgages without a government guarantee.

Creates uniform servicing standards, including a single point of contact for troubled borrowers and an industry-wide model for deciding when to modify a loan instead of foreclosing, plus national standards for the foreclosure process.

Sets federal minimum underwriting standards — verified income and assets, a 5% down payment, and debt-to-income tests — and makes it a violation of federal law for any originator, lender, or loan buyer to finance or purchase a mortgage that fails to meet them.

Directs the FHFA to identify Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac property of value to private entities — historical default databases, home-price indices, securitization technology and patents — and sell it to them, and to shrink the government guarantee on their securities by at least 10% per year.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers who need a low down payment pay first: the 5% minimum (with credit enhancement required below 20% down) applies to FHA-type loans too, since only VA and Rural Housing Service loans are carved out, shrinking the pool of eligible buyers. Investors in the newly exempted securities pay in reduced disclosure protections, and over time ordinary borrowers would bear the cost of losing the GSE guarantee that keeps 30-year mortgage rates low, with no replacement federal backstop specified in the bill.

drawbacks.text: Repeals the Dodd-Frank credit risk retention rule, which required firms bundling loans into securities to keep 5% of the credit risk themselves — removing the incentive to avoid originating loans they did not intend to stand behind.

Exempts mortgage-backed securities backed exclusively by 'deliverable residential mortgages' from Securities Act registration and Exchange Act regulation, cutting disclosure and oversight for investors in those products.

Imposes a nationwide 5% minimum down payment; loans above 80% loan-to-value require credit enhancement, and only VA and Rural Housing Service loans are exempt — so FHA loans, which allow 3.5% down, would be pushed up to a higher barrier for first-time and moderate-income buyers.

Winds down the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guarantee at 10% a year without establishing any replacement federal guarantee, which over time would likely raise mortgage rates and reduce the availability of the 30-year fixed loan most American homebuyers rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles genuinely useful ideas — public loan-level data, uniform servicing and foreclosure standards, one national title database — with a large structural transfer of the mortgage market from a government-backed system to private capital, achieved partly by repealing investor protections (risk retention, securities registration). The borrower protections were real but secondary; the winddown raised rates and credit-access risks for ordinary buyers before any replacement system existed. On balance, the core of the bill served private financial firms more than homebuyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing, and then sat there until the two-year Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Corker introduced the bill on November 9, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee held a single hearing on the bill on November 15, 2011 (printed as S.Hrg. 112-408).
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac kept guaranteeing most new mortgages under conservatorship, banks kept selling loans into that federal guarantee, and low-down-payment FHA lending continued unchanged. No private firm gained the GSE asset sales or the risk-retention repeal, and no borrower lost the 3.5%-down FHA option — but the bill's transparency and servicing standards were also never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and borrowers under the GSE status quo

for.name: Bob Corker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its winddown-of-the-GSEs framework.

against.name: Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: After a single November 2011 hearing, never brought the bill to a committee markup or a Senate vote; it died in committee.

against.name: Real estate, homebuilding, and mortgage industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed rapid winddown of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac without a replacement backstop, arguing it would raise mortgage costs and shrink the buyer pool.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican wrote the bill and one Republican cosponsored it; no Democrat ever signed on, and with no votes ever taken, no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill shrinks their guarantee by 10% a year and orders their proprietary databases, price indices, and patents sold to private firms. Their guarantee keeps 30-year mortgage rates low for ordinary borrowers, but it also concentrates mortgage risk on taxpayers.

They gain the repeal of the 5% risk-retention requirement, an exemption from securities registration for high-quality-loan securities, public loan-level data, and access to GSE assets — while being newly subject to uniform federal underwriting standards they would have to follow for every loan.

Loan-level public data and a uniform pooling and servicing agreement make pricing and comparing securities easier; the securities-law exemption, however, reduces disclosure on some products they would buy.

A uniform pooling and servicing agreement would bind them to a single point of contact for struggling borrowers, a national net-present-value model favoring modification over foreclosure, and standard foreclosure rules — constraining fee-driven servicing practices at borrowers' benefit, while standardization cuts their operating complexity.

A 5% minimum down payment, applied even to FHA-style loans, would shrink the pool of qualified buyers and slow home sales; the industry's interest in a wide buyer pool runs alongside buyers' interest in access to credit.
